title: {{NAME}} and the Night the Fairy Lights Went Out
moral: Sometimes the most heroic thing you can do is simply show up and keep going when everything feels impossible.

pages.content:
The Fairy Lantern District was the jewel of the whole kingdom, a neighbourhood of the smallest possible streets and the tallest possible lights, where ten thousand fairy lanterns hung from gossamer threads and kept the dark at bay every night of the year. Without them, the Moonpath, the migratory route of the Night Swallows, would vanish. The swallows had used it for a thousand years. They trusted it absolutely.

Tonight, every lantern was dark.

{{NAME}} arrived to find Princess Vida standing in the unlit street with a lantern in each hand, both extinguished, her expression the particular kind of composed that means someone is working very hard at not being overwhelmed. The fairies who tended the lanterns were sitting in small miserable clusters on every available ledge and windowsill, their own natural glow reduced to a dim, anxious flicker. Something was draining their light. Something in the air itself, absorbing it as fast as it was produced.

High above, {{NAME}} could hear them: the first advance scouts of the Night Swallow migration, circling in confused loops where the Moonpath should have been, their calls edged with a distress that carried even through the dark. They would tire. They would lose their formation. And the main flock, a hundred thousand birds, was an hour behind them.

pages.content:
The source of the drain was a Hollow, Vida explained, pulling out a precise diagram drawn on birch bark. A Hollow was a kind of void that occasionally formed in old magical districts, a gap in the weave of the enchantment, and it sucked in light the way a drain sucks in water. Harmless normally: they were too small to matter. This one had grown, for reasons still unknown, to three times its normal size, and it had found the district's main magical conduit and parked itself on top of it.

{{NAME}}'s expression, which had been focused and technical, shifted to something more complicated when Vida added the next part. 'You can close a Hollow with sheer willpower,' she said, 'but it pushes back. Equally. The harder you push, the harder it resists. Every hero who has tried it has been pushed away.' She rolled up the diagram. 'But it can be filled, not fought. If enough light is poured into it from multiple sources at once, it reaches saturation point and collapses on itself.'

{{NAME}} looked at the fairies on the windowsills. They looked back, small and tired and dim but very much present. 'You want to use their light,' said {{NAME}}. 'They want to give it,' said Vida. There was a difference, and she knew it, and {{NAME}} understood why she'd said it that way.

pages.content:
The next twenty minutes were the most extraordinary {{NAME}} had ever spent without moving.

The plan was this: {{NAME}} would fly up to the Hollow and hold position directly beneath it, acting as a conductor, a focal point for the fairy light. Vida would coordinate the fairies from the street, directing them in waves, maintaining the rhythm. It was not a contest. It was more like a song that needed many voices to complete.

Flying up to the Hollow, {{NAME}} could feel it immediately: a cold absence that pressed against the suit, against the skin beneath, against something deeper than both. It tasted of nothing, which was worse than tasting of something terrible. It pushed. {{NAME}} pushed back with everything available, not fists or speed or volume, but sheer, stubborn, continued presence. The decision not to leave.

Below, Vida raised her hands and the fairies rose as one. Their natural glow brightened as though they had each made a private decision to override the drain, to simply produce more. They sent their light upward in a directed stream, guided by {{NAME}}'s extended hands, pouring into the Hollow the way sunlight pours into a cold room and changes it.

The Hollow resisted. Then it resisted less. Then it made a sound like a held breath deciding to exhale, and {{NAME}} felt the push reverse: not outward but inward, the Hollow collapsing into itself with a soft, implosive pop that left a warm afterglow in the air where nothing had been.

pages.content:
The lanterns came back on in a sequence that began at the centre of the district and rolled outward like a wave, each lantern lighting in turn as the magical conduit cleared and the fairy-light ran back through the gossamer network like water remembering which way it goes.

From above, flying slowly back down toward the street, {{NAME}} watched it happen and felt the particular sensation of something irreversible being made right. The Moonpath blazed back into existence: a shimmering silver road through the dark sky, exactly where the Night Swallows needed it, exactly when they needed it.

The scout birds found it within seconds. Their calls changed, distress resolving into the clean, navigational calls of creatures who know precisely where they are. And then the main flock arrived: a hundred thousand Night Swallows moving as one living cloud, their wings catching the lantern light and throwing it back a hundred thousand times, flooding the district with a mobile, moving radiance that was neither the lanterns nor the fairy light but something made of both, plus motion, plus the relief of arrival.

Vida watched them with her face turned upward and her crown very straight and both extinguished lanterns now blazing in her hands, and the expression she wore was the exact right expression for the exact moment she was in.

pages.content:
The fairies had recovered their full glow by the time {{NAME}}'s boots touched the street again, and if anything they were a shade brighter than before, as though the act of giving everything had left them with slightly more than they'd started with. Several had taken to following {{NAME}} around the street like a small, festive escort, which was both charming and slightly hard to navigate.

Vida set one of the lanterns down and simply held the other, not for light but because she'd been carrying it all evening and it had become comfortable. 'You stayed up there,' she said, as {{NAME}} landed. 'It pushed and you stayed.' {{NAME}} thought about how to answer that honestly. 'I didn't know how to leave in the middle,' said {{NAME}}. 'I'd said I'd do it, so.' Vida considered this for a long moment. 'That's what it is,' she said quietly. 'That's the whole thing, really.'

The Night Swallows flowed overhead in their great silent river, their migration resumed, their thousand-year route intact. The fairies nested in the lit lanterns and in each other's company, small warm lights in every direction.

{{NAME}} sat on the doorstep of the oldest house in the district and let the warmth settle in, like a fire deciding to stay. Let your own light grow quiet now. Let the lanterns watch over the dark while you sleep. And wonder, softly, what caused the Hollow to grow, because Vida is already starting to find out.
